label: The letter
default:
I've been managing people for over a decade now. Teams of three and teams of 23, managers of other managers, people in their very first job and subject matter experts who'd been in their field for more than 20 years. I've been obsessed with getting better at it the whole way along, and I've tried more systems than I'd like to admit to keep myself organized and make the conversations with the person on the other side of the table (or the Zoom call) genuinely useful.

For most of that time, my system was a Google Doc for every person on the team, and eventually a spreadsheet to keep all the docs straight. It worked fine for a while. Somewhere around seven people it stopped working. Some weeks got written up and a lot didn't, every doc turned into its own unique mess, and I'd walk into a 1:1 or a review running on more memory than I was comfortable with.

I'm a big believer in a good, consistent system, and I lean on data and analysis for most of my decisions, especially when nothing's on fire. When something keeps going sideways on a team, my first guess usually isn't that people need to try harder. It's that the system around them is either missing or way too complicated. So I guess it's not all that surprising that I ended up blending the ops and systems side of me with the part of managing I love most, which is helping people learn, get better at their day-to-day and grow in their careers.

I've never really stopped thinking of myself as a student. Management and Customer Success, sure, but also parenting, history, music, astrophysics and, for some reason, maps. I'm usually reading two or three books at a time (okay, two are audiobooks, but... come on), and most of my podcasts happen on a run or on the bike. Between that, YouTube, conferences and shadowing people who are better at something than I am, I ask a lot of questions. I think being humble enough to know you don't know everything, and soaking up what other people do know, is one of the most important habits you can build. It's also something I try hard to pass on to my teams, so learning and development usually sits front and center in my 1:1s, along with a plan for how that learning turns into the next step in someone's career.

The thing I care about most with anyone on my team is that we're reading from the same sheet of music. They know what's expected of them, they know I know it too, and we both know where things actually stand. When that's in place, feedback lands the way you meant it and the hard conversations get a lot easier. I'd much rather have the slightly awkward conversation in week two than the really awkward one in month six. That's what the name means to me.

Most of my career has been in Customer Success, and I love it. Figuring out how to set a team up so customers really get value from what they're paying for is a puzzle I still enjoy. I've worked on everything from a rapidly changing SaaS product to helping people who spend most of their day a long way from a computer see why a piece of technology is worth their time. Lately that's meant farmers and ranchers, and a team spread across more than one continent, which teaches you pretty quickly to write things down, since half the people you need are asleep when you think of the question.

Outside of work I live in Maine with my family, who come first, full stop (and who've heard every one of my dad jokes at least twice). I'm optimistic to a fault and I try not to take any of it too seriously, which comes in handy when you're building something from scratch.

The Same Page is kind of the culmination of all that. It pulls a handful of tools I'd been cobbling together for myself over the years into one place. My hope is that one day it's more than a piece of software, and becomes a way of managing that helps a lot of people be better at this than I was when I started. If you manage people and something here doesn't match how it goes for you, tell me. I'm sure there are things I've got wrong, and I'd rather hear about them now.
